summary: Proposes new MIME media subtypes, Text/SGML and Application/SGML, for carrying SGML documents. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Name tags for a kind of document so programs know how to handle it.

questions: what is the text/sgml media type
how to label sgml in mime
subtitle: How to label SGML documents in email and on the web.

tldr.problem: SGML documents need a way to be labeled when sent over the internet so systems know how to handle them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1874 proposes two new MIME media types: Text/SGML for human-readable SGML documents, and Application/SGML for others, each with optional parameters for character encoding and transformation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental and these media types were never widely adopted. XML, which is simpler than SGML, became the standard for markup.

today: RFC 1874 remains Experimental and was never upgraded to a higher standards track. SGML itself was superseded by XML, which is simpler and became the standard for markup on the internet.

sections.title: Why SGML Needs a Media Type
sections.content:
The Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML) is a system for describing document structure using tags and rules. Documents built with SGML need a way to be identified when sent over networks, just like HTML documents are identified as "text/html".

RFC 1874 proposes two new MIME media types (the labels attached to documents in email and web transfers) so SGML documents can be properly recognized and processed by the systems that receive them.
sections.plainLanguage: When you download a file from the internet, your computer gets a label that says what kind of file it is. This RFC adds labels for SGML files so computers know how to handle them.

sections.title: The Two SGML Media Types
sections.content:
RFC 1874 defines two media types for SGML documents. The choice between them depends on whether a person can understand the document without special SGML software.

Text/SGML is for SGML documents that are readable as plain text. These documents are structured with SGML markup, but the content is comprehensible to a human without an SGML parser. Each line in the document corresponds to a record in SGML terms.

Application/SGML is for all other SGML documents—those that require SGML software to parse. In these documents, record markers (special characters) are explicitly represented and may not correspond to line breaks.
sections.plainLanguage: Text/SGML is like a book with bookmarks that you can still read even if you ignore the bookmarks. Application/SGML is a file that only makes sense if the computer understands SGML structure.

sections.title: Optional Parameters
sections.content:
Both media types share optional parameters that specify how the document is encoded and what character set it uses.

The charset parameter, such as us-ascii or UTF-8, describes the character encoding. This helps non-SGML systems at least display the text reasonably. SGML-capable systems use the SGML-bctf parameter instead, which specifies a bit combination transformation format—a method for converting the SGML document's bit patterns into the byte sequence in the message. Valid formats include identity (no transformation), fixed-2 through fixed-4 (fixed-width byte sequences), and variable-width formats like UTF-8, UTF-7, and Japanese encodings.

The SGML-boot parameter is used only with document entities (complete SGML documents, not just fragments). It points to another part of the message containing bootstrap information about the document's character set, used when the document uses SGML characters that differ from standard US-ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: These parameters are like instruction labels on a package: they tell the receiver what language the text is in and what special rules are used to encode it.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
SGML documents contain instructions that tell a parser how to interpret the structure and content. A potential risk is that SGML processors may execute arbitrary system commands while parsing a document, similar to the risk with PostScript files.

SGML documents may also contain explicit processing instructions for presentation or composition systems. Recipients of SGML entities should be aware that parsing untrusted SGML documents could trigger unintended system actions.
sections.plainLanguage: SGML documents can contain hidden instructions that might do unexpected things when a program reads them, like a recipe that accidentally tells your kitchen to turn on the stove.

sections.title: Standards Status
sections.content: RFC 1874 is published as an Experimental protocol, meaning it was intended for limited use while the SGML community considered how to encode and transmit SGML documents over the internet. It has not been updated or obsoleted by any later RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC was an experiment to see if SGML documents could be sent over the internet. It was never made into an official standard.
